title: Non-post-secondary graduates
section: Categorical Predictors Ranked by Effect Size (Cramer’s V)
text:
Categorical Predictors Ranked by Effect Size (Cramer’s V)
1. Postsecondary Attendance (V=0.640, 0.275, 0.124) is the strongest categorical predictor by a substantial margin, though the year 1 association is largely structural — driven by the mechanical relationship between attending postsecondary and the attending ps outcome category. Its most substantive and durable finding is that postsecondary attendees show persistently higher sustained statewide employment and lower regional employment relative to non-attendees across all three time points, consistent with the academic pathway.
2. ACT Participation (V=0.302, 0.155, 0.108) is the strongest high school accomplishment predictor and the strongest variable with a clearly substantive rather than structural association at year 1. Its signature — higher postsecondary attendance, lower regional employment, and substantially higher statewide employment — is the clearest expression of the academic pathway among non-college completers and remains the second strongest categorical predictor at every time point.
3. AP Exam Participation (V=0.149, 0.101, 0.065) ranks third, producing a pattern nearly identical to ACT participation in character — high postsecondary attendance early, persistently lower regional and higher statewide employment — but with smaller effect sizes throughout and greater attenuation by year 10.
4. PSEO Participation (V=0.186, 0.072, 0.082) ranks fourth overall, with a strong year 1 association driven by an 18-percentage-point postsecondary attendance gap that dissipates rapidly. Its residual finding — a persistent tendency toward statewide rather than regional employment among PSEO participants who did not complete — mirrors the broader academic pathway pattern but at modest effect sizes at years 5 and 10. Note that this variable is restricted to 2011 cohorts and later.
5. Special Education Status (V=0.171, 0.107, 0.093) is the strongest demographic predictor, distinguished from other demographic variables by its persistent association with employment instability and reduced statewide labor market mobility across all three time points. Its primary signature is not reduced regional employment but rather elevated non-sustained workforce participation and lower statewide employment that endure through year 10.
6. English Learner Status (V=0.140, 0.074, 0.070) ranks sixth, with a strong year 1 association reflecting lower postsecondary attendance and a persistent and growing absence from Minnesota employment records that is its most distinctive feature — differentiating it from other demographic variables and suggesting out-of-state employment, informal work, or geographic departure as plausible explanations.
7. Economic Status (V=0.137, 0.083, 0.091) ranks seventh, with a strong year 1 association again driven largely by differential postsecondary attendance. Its most durable finding is modestly higher sustained statewide employment among non-disadvantaged graduates and greater employment instability among disadvantaged graduates, though the association weakens considerably from year 1 to year 5.
8. CTE Achievement (V=0.094, 0.106, 0.115) is notable as the only accomplishments variable whose effect size grows at every time point, and the strongest categorical predictor oriented toward regional rather than statewide employment. CTE concentrators and completers show progressively higher regional employment and lower no MN employment record rates relative to the no CTE group, with a 15-percentage-point regional employment gap emerging by year 10.
9. Non-English Home Language (V=0.114, 0.068, 0.061) ranks ninth, closely mirroring the English learner pattern in both direction and character but with consistently smaller effect sizes, suggesting that English learner status captures the relevant variation more precisely. Its independent contribution will require evaluation in multivariate models.
10. EDR (V=0.093, 0.103, 0.107) is the strongest high school characteristics predictor, with a growing association driven primarily by a widening gap in sustained statewide employment between EDR 6E (Southwest Central) and the other two EDRs — a geographic labor market differentiation that is largely invisible in the regional employment category, which is similar across all three EDRs.
11. Gender (V=0.058, 0.087, 0.107) ranks eleventh and is distinctive as the only variable whose effect size increases consistently across all three time points. Its growing association reflects a widening gap in sustained regional employment favoring males and an expanding share of females carrying no MN employment record by year 10, suggesting diverging long-term labor market trajectories by gender.
12. Race/Ethnicity (V=0.069, 0.043, 0.054) shows the weakest and least consistent effect sizes of the categorical variables, with American Indian graduates showing a persistently adverse profile and Asian/Pacific Islander graduates displaying a distinctive pattern of high MN record absence alongside relatively high statewide employment among those who remain. Overall effect sizes are small at all three time points.
13. Community Demographic Description (V=0.054, 0.078, 0.094) shows statistically significant but practically weak associations, with the most interpretable pattern being a growing statewide employment advantage for urban/town/rural mix graduates and higher MN record absence among entirely rural graduates. Effect sizes remain too small to add meaningful explanatory value beyond other variables.

title: Non-post-secondary graduates
section: Continuous Predictors Ranked by Effect Size (F-statistic)
text:
Continuous Predictors Ranked by Effect Size (F-statistic)
1. Total CTE Courses Taken (F=146.8, 101.3, 62.1) produces the highest F-statistics of any continuous variable at all three time points. Its pattern is the mirror image of the academic achievement variables: higher CTE course volume is strongly and consistently associated with sustained regional employment, while the no MN employment record group shows persistently the lowest CTE course-taking at every observation window. The three-tier structure at year 10 — regional employment highest, statewide and non-sustained in the middle, no MN record lowest — is among the clearest patterns in the entire analysis.
2. MCA Reading Score (F=144.3, 42.0, 28.0) is the strongest academic achievement measure, consistent with its role as the primary achievement indicator in the full population multivariate models. Its gradient is clear and durable across all three time points: higher scores are associated with statewide employment and — increasingly over time — no MN employment record, while regional employment and non-sustained work form the lowest-scoring tier. F-statistics are the highest of the three MCA measures at years 1 and 5.
3. ACT Composite Score (F=114.2, 44.6, 18.3) ranks third among continuous predictors, producing a pattern consistent with MCA Reading: higher scores associated with postsecondary attendance early and statewide employment later, with regional employment consistently at the lowest-scoring tier. The score gap between sustained statewide and sustained regional employment grows from 0.79 points at year 1 to 1.43 points at year 10, indicating increasing score-based stratification across the observation windows. Note this variable is restricted to ACT takers only.
4. MCA Math Score (F=89.4, 36.0, 34.6) closely mirrors MCA Reading in pattern but with somewhat lower F-statistics at years 1 and 5. Its year 10 F-statistic (34.6) exceeds MCA Reading (28.0), suggesting math achievement carries slightly stronger differentiation at the later time point. The three-tier consolidation at year 10 — statewide and no MN record as a higher-achieving group, regional and non-sustained as a lower-achieving group — replicates the MCA Reading structure.
5. MCA Science Score (F=84.4, 38.1, 25.1) replicates the MCA Reading and Math patterns with high fidelity across all three time points, including the three-tier consolidation at year 10. As in the full population analysis, its voluntary and self-selected nature limits its utility in multivariate models, but its bivariate associations confirm the broader academic achievement gradient and are consistent with retaining MCA Reading as the primary academic achievement indicator.
6. Average County Unemployment Rate (F=31.3, 44.5, 54.7) is notable as the only continuous variable whose F-statistic increases substantially over time, reflecting a growing labor market geography effect. Its most consistent finding is that graduates achieving sustained statewide employment disproportionately originate from higher-unemployment counties — consistent with a labor market push dynamic — while the no MN employment record group shows unemployment rate profiles indistinguishable from sustained regional workers, suggesting out-of-state departure rather than intra-state mobility.
7. Average County Wages as Percent of State Average (F=35.3, 24.0, 26.1) is statistically significant at all three time points but shows very small absolute differences — all contrasts within one to two percentage points of the state average. Its only durable finding mirrors the unemployment rate variable: graduates in sustained statewide employment consistently originate from lower-wage counties. The negligible absolute magnitude of differences limits its practical significance and supports its exclusion from multivariate models.

title: Non-post-secondary graduates
text:
Cross-Cutting Observations
Several themes emerge from the full set of bivariate findings. First, the two-pathway structure identified in the full population analysis is fully present among non-college completers: academic indicators (ACT, AP, PSEO, MCA scores, postsecondary attendance) consistently predict statewide labor market mobility, while CTE indicators (CTE achievement, total CTE courses) predict regional attachment — regardless of whether a credential was earned. Second, the no MN employment record category behaves distinctively across the accomplishment variables, increasingly resembling the statewide employment group on academic achievement measures by years 5 and 10, suggesting that a meaningful share of higher-achieving non-completers have left Minnesota rather than failing to engage with its labor market. Third, demographic variables show weaker associations than accomplishment variables across the board, indicating that what students did in high school is more predictive of workforce participation trajectories than who they are. Finally, several variables — community demographic description, county wages, non-English home language — show statistically significant but practically weak associations unlikely to add explanatory value beyond stronger correlated predictors in multivariate models, consistent with decisions made in the full population analysis.

title: Non-post-secondary graduates
section: The students who were headed somewhere else
text:
The students who were headed somewhere else
Some graduates who ultimately did not complete a postsecondary credential were nonetheless oriented toward college from the start. They took the ACT, participated in AP courses and PSEO, earned higher MCA scores, and went on to attempt postsecondary education even if they didn’t finish it. What happened to them in the labor market looks a lot like what happened to students who did complete degrees — just a dimmer version of the same pattern. They were more likely to leave Southwest Minnesota for employment elsewhere in the state, and by year 10, a striking share of them had simply disappeared from Minnesota employment records entirely. They weren’t failing to find work. The most likely explanation is that they left the state.
This group illustrates something important: academic orientation shapes where people end up even when formal credentials don’t follow. The habits of mind, the networks, the postsecondary experience itself — even an incomplete one — appear to pull people toward broader labor markets and away from the region.

title: Non-post-secondary graduates
section: The students who were built for this place
text:
The students who were built for this place
The other story belongs to graduates with deep CTE engagement. Higher numbers of CTE courses taken, CTE concentrator or completer status — these are the students who showed up in regional employment at year 1 and stayed there. By year 10, CTE concentrators were nearly twice as likely to be in sustained regional employment as graduates with no CTE engagement at all. This isn’t a small finding. It suggests that CTE programs are doing exactly what they are supposed to do for students who engage with them seriously: connecting young people to the regional economy and equipping them to stay.

title: Non-post-secondary graduates
section: The students who fell through the cracks
text:
The students who fell through the cracks
The most troubling pattern in the data belongs to graduates with no CTE engagement and no academic orientation — the students who neither pursued a college track nor developed occupational skills through CTE. By year 10, more than half of graduates with no CTE participation carried no Minnesota employment record at all. This group was already the most likely to have no MN employment record at year 1, and that gap only widened over time. Whether they left the state, work in informal economies, or have simply disengaged from the formal labor market, the data cannot say — but their persistent absence from employment records across a decade is the most concerning finding in the entire analysis.

title: Non-post-secondary graduates
section: The role of identity and circumstance
text:
The role of identity and circumstance
Demographic characteristics — race, gender, economic status, special education status, English learner status — do matter, but they matter less than what students did in high school. Special education students show persistent employment instability. English learners and graduates from non-English speaking homes show elevated absence from Minnesota employment records that grows over time, possibly reflecting employment in sectors that don’t generate wage records or communities that maintain strong ties outside Minnesota. Males are more likely to be in sustained regional employment by year 10; females are increasingly likely to carry no MN employment record. These patterns deserve attention, but they operate in the background of the stronger story told by high school experiences.

title: Non-post-secondary graduates
text:
The geography of opportunity
Where a student went to high school also matters, though modestly. Graduates from EDR 6E — the Southwest Central region anchored by Marshall — show substantially higher rates of employment outside the region compared to graduates from the Upper Minnesota Valley or Southwest EDRs. Graduates from higher- unemployment counties are more likely to leave the region for work elsewhere in the state, consistent with what we would expect when local job markets are tight. But sustained regional employment rates are remarkably similar across the three EDRs, suggesting that the regional economy absorbs similar shares of non-completers regardless of sub-region — it’s the path out of the region that differs.

title: Non-post-secondary graduates
text:
The bottom line
A decade after high school graduation, the non-college completer population has sorted into roughly three groups: those doing steady work in the region, those doing steady work elsewhere, and a large and growing group with no formal Minnesota employment footprint. CTE engagement is the strongest predictor of being in the first group. Academic orientation — even without a credential — predicts the second. And the absence of either, combined with demographic disadvantage, is the clearest signal of the third.
The regional economy depends heavily on workers who choose to stay. This analysis suggests that CTE programs are the most powerful mechanism available for cultivating that attachment among students who will not complete four-year degrees. At the same time, the growing share of non-completers absent from Minnesota employment records by year 10 — many of them higher-achieving graduates who attended postsecondary without finishing — points to an ongoing and unresolved challenge: how to keep talent in a region when the pathways that develop it often point toward somewhere else.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
Summary
Cross-tabulation analysis and one-way ANOVA examined associations between independent variables and postsecondary attendance outcomes (Did not attend PS, Attended - did not grad, Attended - grad) for 47,189 individuals. Variables are presented in two separate ranked lists by effect size measure.
Categorical Variables - Ranked by Cramer’s V

took.ACT (Cramer’s V=0.443) — The strongest categorical predictor. ACT takers show a graduation rate of 67.3% compared to 26.6% for non-takers, with 53.6% of non-takers not attending postsecondary at all.
pseo.participant (Cramer’s V=0.401) — A strong predictor, noting the near-tautological nature of the relationship. PSEO participants show a graduation rate of 76.3% compared to 36.5% for non-participants, with 42.1% of non-participants not attending postsecondary.
economic.status (Cramer’s V=0.299) — Joint strongest demographic predictor alongside special education status. Economically disadvantaged students show a graduation rate of 34.6% compared to 64.4% for non-disadvantaged students, with 42.4% not attending postsecondary.
special.ed.status (Cramer’s V=0.299) — Joint strongest demographic predictor. Special education students show a graduation rate of 21.7% compared to 58.3% for non-special education students, with 59.6% not attending postsecondary.
ap.exam (Cramer’s V=0.230) — A moderate association. AP exam participants show the highest graduation rate of any categorical subgroup examined (79.4%) and the lowest rate of not attending (7.0%).
english.learner (Cramer’s V=0.224) — A moderate association. English learners show a graduation rate of 24.0% compared to 56.3%, with 57.0% not attending postsecondary.
non.english.home (Cramer’s V=0.168) — A weak to moderate association closely mirroring english.learner. Students from non-English speaking homes show a graduation rate of 28.9% compared to 55.7%, with 48.5% not attending.
race.ethnicity (Cramer’s V=0.148) — A weak to moderate association. AI students show the highest rate of not attending (48.6%) while White students show the lowest (22.1%). Asian/PI and Black students show relatively higher graduation rates (42.9% and 39.5% respectively).
gender (Cramer’s V=0.129) — A weak association. Females show a notably higher graduation rate (59.6% vs 47.0%) and lower rate of not attending (23.2% vs 32.7%).
dem.desc (Cramer’s V=0.053) — A very weak association. Entirely rural students show the highest graduation rate (60.9%) and lowest rate of not attending (21.5%).
cte.achievement (Cramer’s V=0.041) — A very weak and inverse association. Higher CTE engagement is modestly associated with lower postsecondary graduation rates, consistent with the workforce pathway sorting mechanism.
edr (Cramer’s V=0.023) — A negligible association. Geographic subregion within Southwest Minnesota has virtually no bearing on postsecondary attendance outcomes.

Continuous Variables - Ranked by Eta-Squared

MCA Reading (η²=0.106) — The strongest continuous predictor with a medium effect. Graduates score significantly higher than non-completers and did not attend PS individuals score significantly lower than both attended groups, with a gap of 0.721 between graduates and non-attendees.
ACT Composite Score (η²=0.094) — A small to medium effect, restricted to ACT takers. The gap between graduates and did not attend PS individuals is very large (estimate=-3.883), reflecting the powerful sorting role of academic achievement in postsecondary pathway selection.
MCA Science (η²=0.088) — A small to medium effect, noting the voluntary and self-selected nature of participation. Pattern mirrors Reading and Math with graduates scoring significantly higher than all other groups.
MCA Math (η²=0.079) — A small to medium effect closely mirroring MCA Reading and Science. Graduates score significantly higher than non-completers and did not attend PS individuals score significantly lower than both attended groups.
avg.unemployment.rate (η²=0.007) — A negligible effect consistent with the opportunity cost hypothesis. Did not attend PS individuals experienced significantly lower average unemployment rates, suggesting favorable local labor market conditions are associated with direct workforce entry.
total.cte.courses.taken (η²=0.008) — A negligible effect. Graduates show significantly fewer CTE courses than non-completers and did not attend PS individuals, further reinforcing the inverse relationship between CTE engagement and postsecondary attendance.
avg.wages.pct.state (η²=0.006) — A negligible effect. Local wage levels explain less than one percent of variance in postsecondary attendance outcomes.

Overall Pattern High school accomplishment variables — particularly took.ACT, pseo.participant, and MCA scores — are the strongest predictors of postsecondary attendance outcomes, considerably stronger than demographic or geographic variables. Among demographic variables, economic status and special education status are the joint strongest predictors, with both showing that disadvantaged groups are primarily distinguished by much higher rates of not attending rather than higher rates of attending without completing, suggesting access rather than completion is the primary barrier. A consistent inverse relationship between CTE engagement and postsecondary attendance across both CTE achievement and total CTE courses taken, combined with negligible geographic effects, reinforces the pathway sorting mechanism in which CTE engagement is associated with direct regional workforce entry rather than postsecondary pursuit. Local labor market conditions show negligible associations, suggesting that individual academic preparation and demographic characteristics are far more powerful determinants of postsecondary attendance than local economic conditions in this regional context.

Ranked by Cramer’s V:
1. Economic Status (Cramer’s V=0.299) The strongest demographic predictor of postsecondary attendance. Non-disadvantaged students show a graduation rate of 64.4% compared to just 34.6% for economically disadvantaged students, while 42.4% of economically disadvantaged students did not attend postsecondary compared to 19.4% of non-disadvantaged students. Economic disadvantage is clearly a substantial barrier to both accessing and completing postsecondary education.
2. Special Education Status (Cramer’s V=0.299) Equally strong as economic status. Special education students show a dramatically lower graduation rate (21.7% vs 58.3%) and a strikingly high rate of not attending postsecondary (59.6% vs 22.9%). Notably, the attended but did not graduate rates are virtually identical between the two groups (18.8% vs 18.8%), suggesting that when special education students do attend they face similar completion challenges to non-special education students but are far less likely to attempt postsecondary in the first place.
3. English Learner Status (Cramer’s V=0.224) A moderate association. English learners show a much lower graduation rate (24.0% vs 56.3%) and a much higher rate of not attending (57.0% vs 24.9%), while attended but did not graduate rates are nearly identical between the two groups (19.0% vs 18.8%), mirroring the pattern observed for special education status.
4. Non-English Home Language (Cramer’s V=0.168) A weak to moderate association closely mirroring the English learner pattern. Students from non-English speaking homes show lower graduation rates (28.9% vs 55.7%) and higher rates of not attending (48.5% vs 25.9%).
5. Gender (Cramer’s V=0.129) A weak association. Females show a notably higher graduation rate (59.6% vs 47.0%) and lower rate of not attending (23.2% vs 32.7%), consistent with well-established national patterns of female postsecondary attainment advantage. The gender gap in graduation rates is notably larger in this dataset than typically observed nationally.
6. Race/Ethnicity (Cramer’s V=0.148) A weak to moderate association with notable variation across groups. AI students show the highest rate of not attending (48.6%) while White students show the lowest (22.1%). Asian/PI and Black students show relatively higher graduation rates (42.9% and 39.5% respectively) compared to AI (24.7%) and Hispanic (26.5%) students. Small sample sizes for minority groups warrant cautious interpretation.
Summary Economic status and special education status are the joint strongest demographic predictors of postsecondary attendance outcomes (both Cramer’s V=0.299), with both variables showing large differences in graduation rates and not attending rates. A consistent and important pattern across economic status, special education, English learner, and non-English home language variables is that disadvantaged groups are primarily distinguished by much higher rates of not attending rather than higher rates of attending without graduating — the attended but did not graduate rates are nearly identical across all disadvantaged and non-disadvantaged groups — suggesting that access rather than completion is the primary barrier for these groups. Gender shows a weak but substantively meaningful association with females showing considerably higher graduation rates than males.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
High School Characteristics
Here are the variables we will be testing;

High school characteristics

Dem_Desc
edr
avg.unemp.rate
avg.wage.pct.state




Summary
Overview Cross-tabulation analysis and one-way ANOVA examined the relationship between high school characteristics and local labor market variables and postsecondary attendance outcomes (Did not attend PS, Attended - did not grad, Attended - grad) for 47,189 individuals. Categorical variables are ranked by Cramer’s V and continuous variables by eta-squared.
Categorical Variables - Ranked by Cramer’s V
1. Community Demographic Description (Cramer’s V=0.053) A very weak but statistically significant association. Entirely rural students show the highest graduation rate (60.9%) and the lowest rate of not attending (21.5%), while town/rural mix students show the lowest graduation rate (51.2%) and the highest rate of not attending (29.8%). Urban/town/rural mix students fall in between (55.1% graduated, 26.0% did not attend). Attended but did not graduate rates are nearly identical across all three community types (17-19%), suggesting that community type influences the decision to attend rather than completion once enrolled.
2. EDR (Cramer’s V=0.023) A negligible association. Graduation rates are nearly identical across EDR 6E Southwest Central (51.5%), EDR 6W Upper Minnesota Valley (52.9%), and EDR 8 Southwest (54.5%), as are rates of not attending (29.2%, 29.1%, and 26.7% respectively). Geographic subregion within Southwest Minnesota has virtually no bearing on postsecondary attendance outcomes.
Continuous Variables - Ranked by Eta-Squared
1. Average Unemployment Rate (η²=0.007) A negligible effect size despite statistical significance. Tukey HSD post-hoc tests reveal that did not attend PS individuals experienced significantly lower average unemployment rates than both attended groups (estimate= -0.303 vs did not grad, p<0.001; estimate=-0.218 vs grad, p<0.001), consistent with the opportunity cost hypothesis — favorable local labor market conditions are associated with direct workforce entry rather than postsecondary attendance. The difference between the two attended groups is smaller but significant (estimate=-0.085, p<0.001).
2. Average Wages as Percentage of State Average (η²=0.006) A negligible effect size. Tukey HSD post-hoc tests show that graduates experience slightly higher relative wages than non-completers (estimate=0.004, p<0.001), while did not attend PS individuals experience significantly lower relative wages than both attended groups, consistent with the opportunity cost hypothesis but with a very small practical effect.
Summary High school characteristics and labor market variables show negligible to very weak associations with postsecondary attendance outcomes. EDR shows a negligible association, confirming that geographic subregion within Southwest Minnesota has virtually no bearing on postsecondary attendance decisions. Community demographic description shows a slightly stronger but still very weak association, with entirely rural students showing the highest graduation rates. Both labor market variables show associations consistent with the opportunity cost hypothesis but with negligible effect sizes, suggesting that local labor market conditions play a very modest role in postsecondary attendance decisions in this regional context.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
High School Accomplishments
Here are the variables we are exploring;

High school accomplishments

took.ACT
ACTCompositeScore
ap.exam
pseo.participant
cte.achievement
total.cte.courses.taken
MCA.M
MCA.R
MCA.S




Summary
Overview Cross-tabulation analysis and one-way ANOVA examined the relationship between high school accomplishment variables and postsecondary attendance outcomes (Did not attend PS, Attended - did not grad, Attended - grad) for 47,189 individuals, with the exception of pseo.participant which excludes the 2008-2010 graduation cohorts. Categorical variables are ranked by Cramer’s V and continuous variables by eta-squared.
Categorical Variables - Ranked by Cramer’s V
1. took.ACT (Cramer’s V=0.443) The strongest categorical predictor of postsecondary attendance. Students who took the ACT show a graduation rate of 67.3% compared to just 26.6% for non-ACT takers, while 53.6% of non-ACT students did not attend postsecondary compared to only 14.4% of ACT takers. This is the largest differential observed across any categorical variable examined for postsecondary attendance.
2. pseo.participant (Cramer’s V=0.401) The second strongest categorical predictor. PSEO participants show a graduation rate of 76.3% compared to 36.5% for non-participants, while 42.1% of non-participants did not attend postsecondary compared to only 10.8% of PSEO participants. The near-tautological nature of this relationship should be noted — PSEO participants are by definition already engaged in college coursework while in high school.
3. ap.exam (Cramer’s V=0.230) A moderate association. AP exam participants show a graduation rate of 79.4% — the highest of any categorical subgroup examined — and a very low rate of not attending (7.0%), while non-AP exam students show a lower graduation rate (48.6%) and higher rate of not attending (31.7%).
4. cte.achievement (Cramer’s V=0.041) A very weak association. Graduation rates show a modest inverse relationship with CTE engagement level — No CTE students show the highest graduation rate (56.4%), followed by CTE Participants (55.2%) and CTE Concentrators or Completors (50.6%). Higher CTE engagement is modestly associated with lower postsecondary graduation rates, consistent with the workforce pathway sorting mechanism identified throughout this analysis.
Continuous Variables - Ranked by Eta-Squared
1. MCA Reading (η²=0.106) The strongest continuous predictor with a medium effect size. Graduates score significantly higher than non-completers (estimate=0.333, p<0.001), while did not attend PS individuals score significantly lower than both attended groups (estimate=-0.388 vs did not grad, p<0.001; estimate=-0.721 vs grad, p<0.001). The large gap between graduates and did not attend PS individuals confirms Reading achievement as the strongest continuous predictor of postsecondary pathway.
2. ACT Composite Score (η²=0.094) A small to medium effect size, restricted to ACT takers. Graduates show substantially higher ACT scores than non-completers (estimate=2.035, p<0.001), while did not attend PS individuals show significantly lower scores than both non-completers (estimate= -1.848, p<0.001) and graduates (estimate=-3.883, p<0.001). The very large gap between graduates and did not attend PS individuals reflects the powerful sorting role of academic achievement in postsecondary pathway selection.
3. MCA Science (η²=0.088) A small to medium effect size, noting the voluntary and self-selected nature of Science MCA participation. Graduates show significantly higher Science scores than non-completers (estimate=0.346, p<0.001) and did not attend PS individuals show significantly lower scores than both attended groups (estimate= -0.264 vs did not grad, p<0.001; estimate=-0.611 vs grad, p<0.001).
4. MCA Math (η²=0.079) A small to medium effect size mirroring the MCA Reading and Science patterns. Graduates score significantly higher than non-completers (estimate=0.422, p<0.001) and did not attend PS individuals score significantly lower than graduates (estimate=-0.668, p<0.001) and non-completers (estimate=-0.246, p<0.001).
5. Total CTE Courses Taken (η²=0.008) A negligible effect size despite statistical significance. Graduates show significantly fewer CTE courses than non-completers (estimate=-0.668, p<0.001), while no significant difference is found between did not attend PS and non-completers (p=0.526). Did not attend PS individuals show significantly more CTE courses than graduates (estimate=0.726, p<0.001), consistent with the inverse relationship between CTE engagement and postsecondary attendance identified throughout this analysis.
Summary High school accomplishment variables show the strongest associations with postsecondary attendance outcomes of any variable group examined. took.ACT, pseo.participant, and all three MCA scores show meaningful effect sizes, with MCA Reading emerging as the strongest continuous predictor (η²=0.106). A clear and consistent pattern emerges across both categorical and continuous variables — academic achievement and college preparedness indicators are strongly associated with postsecondary attendance and completion, while CTE engagement shows a modest inverse relationship. The negligible effect of total CTE courses taken on postsecondary attendance, combined with its meaningful association with regional workforce participation identified earlier, further reinforces the distinct and complementary nature of academic and CTE pathways in Southwest Minnesota.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
Summary
Cross-tabulation analysis and one-way ANOVA examined associations between independent variables and postsecondary graduation (College completer vs Non-college completer) for 47,189 individuals. Variables are presented in two separate ranked lists by effect size measure. Binary categorical variables report phi (φ) and multi-category variables report Cramer’s V.
Categorical Variables - Ranked by Effect Size

took.ACT (φ=0.389) — Joint strongest categorical predictor alongside pseo.participant. ACT takers show a completion rate of 67.3% compared to 26.6% for non-takers, with non-ACT takers showing a non-completion rate of 73.4%.
pseo.participant (φ=0.389) — Joint strongest categorical predictor. PSEO participants show a completion rate of 76.3% compared to 36.5% for non-participants, noting the near- tautological nature of this relationship.
economic.status (φ=0.289) — The strongest demographic predictor. Non-disadvantaged students show a completion rate of 64.4% compared to 34.6% for economically disadvantaged students, a gap of nearly 30 percentage points.
special.ed.status (φ=0.256) — The second strongest demographic predictor. Special education students show a completion rate of just 21.7% compared to 58.3% for non-special education students, the lowest completion rate of any demographic subgroup examined.
ap.exam (φ=0.220) — A moderate association. AP exam participants show the highest completion rate of any categorical subgroup examined (79.4%) compared to 48.6% for non-AP exam students.
race.ethnicity (Cramer’s V=0.200) — A moderate association. White students show the highest completion rate (59.0%) while AI students show the lowest (24.7%), with a non-completion rate of 75.3%.
english.learner (φ=0.193) — A moderate association. English learners show a completion rate of 24.0% compared to 56.3% for non-English learners, one of the largest completion rate differentials observed across all demographic variables.
non.english.home (φ=0.158) — A weak to moderate association closely mirroring english.learner. Students from non-English speaking homes show a completion rate of 28.9% compared to 55.7%.
gender (φ=0.126) — A weak association. Females show a notably higher completion rate (59.6% vs 47.0%), consistent with well-established national patterns of female postsecondary attainment advantage.
dem.desc (Cramer’s V=0.070) — A very weak association. Entirely rural students show the highest completion rate (60.9%) while town/rural mix students show the lowest (51.2%).
cte.achievement (Cramer’s V=0.052) — A very weak and inverse association. No CTE students show the highest completion rate (56.4%) while CTE Concentrators or Completors show the lowest (50.6%), consistent with the workforce pathway sorting mechanism.
edr (Cramer’s V=0.027) — A negligible association. Completion rates are nearly identical across all three EDRs, confirming that geographic subregion has virtually no bearing on postsecondary graduation outcomes.

Continuous Variables - Ranked by Eta-Squared

MCA Reading (η²=0.087) — The strongest continuous predictor with a small to medium effect. College completers score significantly higher than non-completers (estimate=0.555), confirming Reading achievement as the strongest MCA predictor of postsecondary graduation.
ACT Composite Score (η²=0.082) — A small to medium effect restricted to ACT takers. College completers show substantially higher ACT scores than non-completers (estimate=2.847), reflecting the strong relationship between academic achievement and postsecondary completion.
MCA Science (η²=0.078) — A small to medium effect, noting the voluntary and self-selected nature of participation. College completers score significantly higher than non-completers (estimate=0.501).
MCA Math (η²=0.073) — A small to medium effect mirroring Reading and Science. College completers score significantly higher than non-completers (estimate=0.563).
avg.wages.pct.state (η²=0.004) — A negligible effect. College completers experience slightly higher relative wages, consistent with the expectation that graduates enter higher-wage labor markets but with virtually no practical predictive value.
avg.unemployment.rate (η²=0.001) — A negligible effect. College completers experienced slightly higher local unemployment rates, consistent with the opportunity cost hypothesis but with essentially zero practical predictive value.
total.cte.courses.taken (η²=0.008) — A negligible effect. Non-completers show significantly more CTE courses than completers (estimate=0.703), consistent with the inverse relationship between CTE engagement and postsecondary completion observed throughout this analysis.

Overall Pattern The predictors of postsecondary graduation closely mirror those of postsecondary attendance, with academic achievement and college preparedness variables dominating and demographic disadvantage variables showing moderate to strong associations. The most notable finding unique to postsecondary graduation is that MCA Reading emerges as the strongest continuous predictor, suggesting reading proficiency is particularly important for credential completion beyond mere enrollment. Geographic variables continue to show negligible associations, confirming that individual-level academic preparation and demographic characteristics — not geographic origin within Southwest Minnesota — are the primary drivers of postsecondary graduation outcomes. The consistent inverse relationship between CTE engagement and postsecondary graduation across both CTE achievement and total CTE courses taken reinforces the distinct and complementary nature of academic and CTE pathways throughout this analysis.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
Demographics

Summary
Overview Cross-tabulation analysis examined the relationship between demographic variables and postsecondary graduation (College completer vs Non-college completer) for 47,189 individuals. Binary variables report phi (φ), which is equivalent to Cramer’s V for 2x2 tables. Variables are ranked by effect size from strongest to weakest association.
Ranked by Effect Size:
1. Economic Status (φ=0.289) The strongest demographic predictor of postsecondary graduation. Non-disadvantaged students show a completion rate of 64.4% compared to just 34.6% for economically disadvantaged students — a gap of nearly 30 percentage points. Economic disadvantage is clearly the most powerful demographic barrier to postsecondary completion in this dataset.
2. Special Education Status (φ=0.256) The second strongest demographic predictor. Special education students show a dramatically lower completion rate (21.7% vs 58.3%), the lowest of any demographic subgroup examined. The nearly 37 percentage point gap between special education and non-special education students is the largest differential observed across any binary demographic variable.
3. Race/Ethnicity (Cramer’s V=0.200) A moderate association with notable variation across groups. White students show the highest completion rate (59.0%), followed by Asian/PI (42.9%) and Black (39.5%) students. AI (24.7%) and Hispanic (26.5%) students show the lowest completion rates, with AI students showing a non-completion rate of 75.3% — the highest of any racial/ethnic group. Small sample sizes for minority groups warrant cautious interpretation.
4. English Learner Status (φ=0.193) A moderate association. English learners show a completion rate of just 24.0% compared to 56.3% for non-English learners, a gap of over 32 percentage points. This is one of the largest completion rate differentials observed across all demographic variables, suggesting English learner status is a substantial barrier to postsecondary completion.
5. Non-English Home Language (φ=0.158) A weak to moderate association closely mirroring the English learner pattern. Students from non-English speaking homes show a completion rate of 28.9% compared to 55.7%, a gap of nearly 27 percentage points.
6. Gender (φ=0.126) The weakest demographic predictor. Females show a notably higher completion rate (59.6% vs 47.0%), a gap of nearly 13 percentage points. This gender gap in postsecondary completion is consistent with well-established national patterns and is one of the more substantively important findings given its implications for regional workforce development.
Summary Economic status and special education status are the strongest demographic predictors of postsecondary graduation, both showing gaps of over 30 percentage points between advantaged and disadvantaged groups. Race/ethnicity shows a moderate association with particularly low completion rates for AI and Hispanic students. English learner status and non-English home language show moderate associations with large completion rate differentials, suggesting language barriers are a significant obstacle to postsecondary completion. Gender shows the weakest association but in a substantively important direction, with females showing considerably higher completion rates than males across all groups examined.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
High School Characteristics

Summary
Overview Cross-tabulation analysis and one-way ANOVA examined the relationship between high school characteristics and local labor market variables and postsecondary graduation (College completer vs Non-college completer) for 47,189 individuals. Categorical variables are ranked by Cramer’s V and continuous variables by eta-squared.
Categorical Variables - Ranked by Cramer’s V
1. Community Demographic Description (Cramer’s V=0.070) A very weak but statistically significant association. Entirely rural students show the highest completion rate (60.9%), followed by urban/town/rural mix (55.1%) and town/rural mix (51.2%) students. The difference between entirely rural and town/rural mix students is modest at approximately 10 percentage points, suggesting that community type plays a very limited role in postsecondary completion once students have enrolled.
2. EDR (Cramer’s V=0.027) A negligible association. Completion rates are nearly identical across EDR 6E Southwest Central (51.5%), EDR 6W Upper Minnesota Valley (52.9%), and EDR 8 Southwest (54.5%). Geographic subregion within Southwest Minnesota has virtually no bearing on postsecondary graduation outcomes.
Continuous Variables - Ranked by Eta-Squared
1. Average Wages as Percentage of State Average (η²=0.004) A negligible effect size despite statistical significance. College completers experience significantly higher average wages than non-completers (estimate=0.009, p<0.001), consistent with the expectation that postsecondary graduates enter higher-wage labor markets. However the effect size is negligible, suggesting local wage levels at the time of high school graduation explain very little variance in eventual postsecondary completion.
2. Average Unemployment Rate (η²=0.001) A negligible effect size. College completers experienced significantly higher average unemployment rates than non-completers (estimate=-0.096, p<0.001), suggesting that individuals who completed postsecondary education tended to come from areas with slightly higher unemployment — consistent with the opportunity cost hypothesis where higher unemployment reduces the attractiveness of immediate workforce entry. However the effect size is essentially zero in practical terms.
Summary High school characteristics and labor market variables show negligible to very weak associations with postsecondary graduation outcomes, the weakest of any variable group examined for this outcome. EDR shows a negligible association, confirming that geographic subregion within Southwest Minnesota has no meaningful bearing on postsecondary graduation. Community demographic description shows a very weak association with entirely rural students showing slightly higher completion rates. Both labor market variables show negligible effect sizes, suggesting that local economic conditions at the time of high school graduation have virtually no practical influence on whether individuals ultimately complete a postsecondary credential.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
High School Accomplishments

Summary
Overview Cross-tabulation analysis and one-way ANOVA examined the relationship between high school accomplishment variables and postsecondary graduation (College completer vs Non-college completer) for 47,189 individuals, with the exception of pseo.participant which excludes the 2008-2010 graduation cohorts. Binary categorical variables report phi (φ) and multi-category variables report Cramer’s V. Continuous variables are ranked by eta-squared.
Categorical Variables - Ranked by Effect Size
1. took.ACT (φ=0.389) The joint strongest categorical predictor alongside pseo.participant. ACT takers show a completion rate of 67.3% compared to just 26.6% for non-ACT takers — a gap of over 40 percentage points, the largest differential observed across any categorical variable for postsecondary graduation. Non-ACT takers show a non-completion rate of 73.4%, suggesting that not taking the ACT is a very strong signal of postsecondary non-completion.
2. pseo.participant (φ=0.389) Equally strong as took.ACT. PSEO participants show a completion rate of 76.3% compared to 36.5% for non-participants — a gap of nearly 40 percentage points. Given the near-tautological nature of this relationship, the association should be interpreted with the understanding that PSEO participants are already in a postsecondary pathway while still in high school.
3. ap.exam (φ=0.220) A moderate association. AP exam participants show a completion rate of 79.4% — the highest of any categorical subgroup examined — compared to 48.6% for non-AP exam students, a gap of nearly 31 percentage points.
4. cte.achievement (Cramer’s V=0.052) A very weak association with an interesting inverse pattern. No CTE students show the highest completion rate (56.4%), followed by CTE Participants (55.2%) and CTE Concentrators or Completors (50.6%). The differences are modest but consistent with the broader pathway sorting mechanism — higher CTE engagement is modestly associated with lower postsecondary completion rates, likely reflecting the direct workforce entry pathway associated with intensive CTE engagement.
Continuous Variables - Ranked by Eta-Squared
1. MCA Reading (η²=0.087) The strongest continuous predictor with a small to medium effect. College completers score significantly higher than non-completers (estimate=0.555, p<0.001), confirming that Reading achievement is the strongest MCA predictor of postsecondary graduation.
2. ACT Composite Score (η²=0.082) A small to medium effect restricted to ACT takers. College completers show substantially higher ACT scores than non-completers (estimate=2.847, p<0.001), reflecting the well-established relationship between academic achievement and postsecondary completion.
3. MCA Science (η²=0.078) A small to medium effect, noting the voluntary and self-selected nature of Science MCA participation. College completers score significantly higher than non-completers (estimate=0.501, p<0.001).
4. MCA Math (η²=0.073) A small to medium effect closely mirroring MCA Reading and Science. College completers score significantly higher than non-completers (estimate=0.563, p<0.001).
5. Total CTE Courses Taken (η²=0.008) A negligible effect size despite statistical significance. Non-completers show significantly more CTE courses than completers (estimate=0.703, p<0.001), consistent with the inverse relationship between CTE engagement and postsecondary completion observed throughout this analysis.
Summary High school accomplishment variables show strong to moderate associations with postsecondary graduation outcomes, with took.ACT and pseo.participant tied as the strongest categorical predictors (both φ=0.389) and MCA Reading emerging as the strongest continuous predictor (η²=0.087). The patterns closely mirror those observed for postsecondary attendance, with academic achievement and college preparedness indicators strongly associated with completion and CTE engagement showing a modest inverse relationship. The negligible effect of total CTE courses taken on graduation, combined with its meaningful association with regional workforce participation, continues to reinforce the complementary nature of academic and CTE pathways in Southwest Minnesota.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
Summary
Cross-tabulation analysis and one-way ANOVA examined associations between independent variables and highest credential level attained (Bachelor degree or higher vs Sub-baccalaureate degree) among the 24,998 college completers in the dataset. Variables are presented in two separate ranked lists by effect size measure. Binary categorical variables report phi (φ) and multi-category variables report Cramer’s V.
Categorical Variables - Ranked by Effect Size

took.ACT (φ=0.360) — The strongest categorical predictor. ACT takers show a bachelor degree or higher rate of 67.6% compared to just 21.0% for non-takers, with non-ACT completers overwhelmingly concentrated in sub-baccalaureate credentials (79.0%).
pseo.participant (φ=0.311) — The second strongest categorical predictor. PSEO participants show a bachelor degree or higher rate of 71.4% compared to 40.4% for non-participants, suggesting early college exposure is strongly associated with higher credential attainment.
ap.exam (φ=0.262) — A moderate to strong association. AP exam participants show the highest bachelor degree or higher rate of any categorical subgroup (83.5%), with only 16.5% attaining a sub-baccalaureate credential.
cte.achievement (Cramer’s V=0.219) — A moderate association with the clearest dose-response pattern observed across any outcome. No CTE completers show the highest bachelor degree or higher rate (74.8%), declining to 65.0% for CTE Participants and 48.9% for CTE Concentrators or Completors. Higher CTE engagement is strongly associated with sub- baccalaureate rather than bachelor degree or higher attainment.
economic.status (φ=0.188) — The strongest demographic predictor. Non-disadvantaged completers show a bachelor degree or higher rate of 64.7% compared to 43.3% for economically disadvantaged completers.
special.ed.status (φ=0.206) — A strong demographic predictor. Special education completers show a bachelor degree or higher rate of just 18.5% compared to 62.0% for non-special education completers, the most extreme differential observed across any demographic variable.
race.ethnicity (Cramer’s V=0.116) — A weak association. Hispanic completers show the lowest bachelor degree or higher rate (36.1%) while White completers show the highest (63.9%). AI, Asian/PI, and Black completers show similar rates of approximately 51-53%.
english.learner (φ=0.148) — A weak to moderate association. English learner completers show a bachelor degree or higher rate of just 25.8% compared to 61.0% for non-English learner completers.
non.english.home (φ=0.121) — A weak association mirroring english.learner. Students from non-English speaking homes show a bachelor degree or higher rate of 34.1% compared to 60.8%.
gender (φ=0.109) — A weak association. Female completers show a higher bachelor degree or higher rate (64.4% vs 53.6%), consistent with national patterns of female postsecondary attainment advantage.
edr (Cramer’s V=0.070) — A very weak association. EDR 6E Southwest Central completers show the highest bachelor degree or higher rate (62.9%) while EDR 6W Upper Minnesota Valley completers show the lowest (53.2%).
dem.desc (Cramer’s V=0.056) — A very weak association. Urban/town/rural mix completers show the highest bachelor degree or higher rate (65.2%) while entirely rural completers show the lowest (55.8%).

Continuous Variables - Ranked by Eta-Squared

ACT Composite Score (η²=0.167) — The strongest continuous predictor with a large effect size — the largest observed for any continuous variable across all outcomes examined. Bachelor degree or higher completers score substantially higher than sub- baccalaureate completers (estimate=3.887).
MCA Reading (η²=0.118) — A medium to large effect. Bachelor degree or higher completers score significantly higher than sub-baccalaureate completers (estimate=0.541).
MCA Science (η²=0.101) — A medium effect, noting the voluntary nature of participation. Bachelor degree or higher completers score significantly higher (estimate=0.526).
Total CTE Courses Taken (η²=0.084) — A small to medium effect and notably stronger than for previous outcomes. Sub-baccalaureate completers take significantly more CTE courses than bachelor degree or higher completers (estimate=2.226), confirming CTE engagement is associated with shorter-term credential attainment.
MCA Math (η²=0.081) — A small to medium effect mirroring Reading and Science. Bachelor degree or higher completers score significantly higher (estimate=0.546).
avg.unemployment.rate (η²=0.005) — A negligible effect. Bachelor degree or higher completers experienced slightly higher local unemployment rates, consistent with the opportunity cost hypothesis.
avg.wages.pct.state (η²=0.000) — Not statistically significant (p=0.071). Local wage levels have no meaningful association with credential level among completers.

Overall Pattern Academic achievement and college preparedness variables dominate the prediction of credential level among completers, with ACT composite score showing the largest effect size observed for any continuous variable across all outcomes examined in this analysis. The most substantively important finding is the strong, consistent, and inverse relationship between CTE engagement and bachelor degree or higher attainment — both cte.achievement and total CTE courses taken show meaningful associations with sub-baccalaureate credentials among completers, the strongest evidence yet for the distinct and complementary nature of CTE and academic pathways in Southwest Minnesota. Demographic disadvantage variables continue to show meaningful associations, with special education status and economic status showing particularly large differentials in credential level attainment. Geographic variables remain weak to negligible, confirming that individual-level academic preparation and demographic characteristics are the primary determinants of credential level among college completers in this region.

                                     ifelse(highest.cred.level %in% c("Bachelor degree", "Master degree or higher"), "Bachelor degree or higher", highest.cred.level)),

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
Demographics

Summary
Overview Cross-tabulation analysis examined the relationship between demographic variables and highest credential level attained (Bachelor degree or higher vs Sub-baccalaureate degree) among the 24,998 college completers in the dataset. This analysis addresses which demographic characteristics are associated with attaining higher versus lower credential levels among those who successfully complete postsecondary education. Binary variables report phi (φ) and multi-category variables report Cramer’s V.
Ranked by Effect Size:
1. Special Education Status (φ=0.206) The strongest demographic predictor of credential level among college completers. Special education completers show a bachelor degree or higher rate of just 18.5% compared to 62.0% for non-special education completers — a gap of over 43 percentage points, the largest differential observed across any demographic variable. When special education students do complete postsecondary education, they are overwhelmingly likely to attain a sub-baccalaureate credential (81.5%), suggesting their postsecondary pathway is strongly oriented toward shorter-term credentials.
2. Economic Status (φ=0.188) The second strongest demographic predictor. Non- disadvantaged completers show a bachelor degree or higher rate of 64.7% compared to 43.3% for economically disadvantaged completers — a gap of over 21 percentage points. Economic disadvantage not only reduces the likelihood of attending and completing postsecondary education but also shapes the type of credential attained among those who do complete.
3. English Learner Status (φ=0.148) A weak to moderate association. English learner completers show a bachelor degree or higher rate of just 25.8% compared to 61.0% for non-English learner completers — a gap of over 35 percentage points. English learners who do complete postsecondary are heavily concentrated in sub-baccalaureate credentials (74.2%), suggesting strong orientation toward shorter-term vocational pathways even among completers.
4. Race/Ethnicity (Cramer’s V=0.116) A weak association with a notable pattern. Hispanic completers show the lowest bachelor degree or higher rate (36.1%), substantially below AI (51.1%), Black (52.8%), and Asian/PI (53.3%) completers. White completers show the highest rate (63.9%). The relatively similar rates across AI, Asian/PI, and Black completers — all approximately 51-53% — is a notable finding suggesting that among completers these groups face similar credential attainment trajectories. Small sample sizes for minority groups warrant cautious interpretation.
5. Non-English Home Language (φ=0.121) A weak association closely mirroring the English learner pattern. Students from non-English speaking homes who complete postsecondary show a bachelor degree or higher rate of 34.1% compared to 60.8% for English speaking home completers, with 65.9% of non-English home completers attaining only a sub-baccalaureate credential.
6. Gender (φ=0.109) The weakest demographic predictor. Female completers show a notably higher bachelor degree or higher rate (64.4% vs 53.6%), a gap of nearly 11 percentage points. This gender gap in credential level among completers is consistent with national patterns and reinforces the broader finding that females show stronger postsecondary outcomes than males at every stage of the pathway.
Summary Among college completers, special education status and economic status are the strongest demographic predictors of credential level attained. A consistent and substantively important pattern across special education status, English learner status, and non-English home language is that disadvantaged groups who do complete postsecondary are heavily concentrated in sub-baccalaureate credentials, suggesting these groups face compounding barriers — first in accessing postsecondary education, and then in attaining higher-level credentials even when they do complete. Gender shows the weakest association but in a consistent direction, with females showing higher bachelor degree or higher rates across all groups examined.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
High School Characteristics

Summary
Highest Credential Level
Overview Cross-tabulation analysis and one-way ANOVA examined the relationship between high school characteristics and local labor market variables and highest credential level attained (Bachelor degree or higher vs Sub-baccalaureate degree) among the 24,998 college completers in the dataset.
Categorical Variables - Ranked by Cramer’s V
1. EDR (Cramer’s V=0.070) A very weak but statistically significant association. EDR 6E Southwest Central completers show the highest bachelor degree or higher rate (62.9%), followed by EDR 8 Southwest (59.4%) and EDR 6W Upper Minnesota Valley (53.2%). The nearly 10 percentage point gap between EDR 6E and EDR 6W is the most notable geographic difference observed, suggesting that completers from the Southwest Central subregion are somewhat more likely to attain higher-level credentials, possibly reflecting the influence of Marshall and other larger urban centers with access to 4-year institution pathways.
2. Community Demographic Description (Cramer’s V=0.056) A very weak association. Urban/town/rural mix completers show the highest bachelor degree or higher rate (65.2%), followed by town/rural mix (59.0%) and entirely rural (55.8%) completers. The pattern suggests a modest urban gradient in credential level attainment among completers, with more urban communities associated with higher-level credentials, likely reflecting greater proximity to and familiarity with 4-year institutions.
Continuous Variables - Ranked by Eta-Squared
1. Average Unemployment Rate (η²=0.005) A negligible effect size. Bachelor degree or higher completers experienced significantly higher average unemployment rates than sub-baccalaureate completers (estimate=-0.186, p<0.001), consistent with the opportunity cost hypothesis — individuals from higher unemployment areas may be more likely to pursue longer-term credential pathways given fewer immediate employment alternatives.
2. Average Wages as Percentage of State Average (η²=0.000) Not statistically significant (p=0.071). Local wage levels at the time of high school graduation show no meaningful association with eventual credential level among completers.
Summary High school characteristics and labor market variables show very weak to negligible associations with credential level attained among college completers. Both EDR and community demographic description show very weak associations with modest urban gradients — completers from more urban and centrally located communities show slightly higher rates of bachelor degree or higher attainment. Average unemployment rate shows a negligible but statistically significant association consistent with the opportunity cost hypothesis, while average wages show no significant association. Overall, geographic and local labor market factors play a very limited role in determining credential level among those who do complete postsecondary education, suggesting that individual- level factors are far more important determinants of credential attainment.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
High School Accomplishments

Summary
Overview Cross-tabulation analysis and one-way ANOVA examined the relationship between high school accomplishment variables and highest credential level attained (Bachelor degree or higher vs Sub-baccalaureate degree) among the 24,998 college completers in the dataset, with the exception of pseo.participant which excludes the 2008-2010 graduation cohorts. This analysis reveals which high school accomplishment variables are most strongly associated with attaining higher versus lower credential levels among those who do complete postsecondary education.
Categorical Variables - Ranked by Effect Size
1. took.ACT (φ=0.360) The strongest categorical predictor of credential level among completers. ACT takers show a bachelor degree or higher rate of 67.6% compared to just 21.0% for non-ACT takers — a gap of nearly 47 percentage points, the largest differential observed across any variable for this outcome. Non-ACT completers are heavily concentrated in sub-baccalaureate credentials (79.0%), suggesting that when non-ACT takers do complete postsecondary they overwhelmingly attain shorter-term credentials.
2. pseo.participant (φ=0.311) The second strongest categorical predictor. PSEO participants show a bachelor degree or higher rate of 71.4% compared to 40.4% for non-participants — a gap of 31 percentage points. This is one of the most substantively important findings for this outcome, as it suggests that early college exposure through PSEO is strongly associated with attainment of higher-level credentials among completers.
3. ap.exam (φ=0.262) A moderate to strong association. AP exam participants show a bachelor degree or higher rate of 83.5% — the highest of any categorical subgroup examined for this outcome — compared to 52.6% for non-AP exam students. Only 16.5% of AP exam participants who complete postsecondary attain a sub- baccalaureate credential, suggesting AP exam participation is a very strong signal of bachelor degree or higher attainment among completers.
4. cte.achievement (Cramer’s V=0.219) A moderate association with a notably clear and inverse dose-response pattern. No CTE completers show the highest bachelor degree or higher rate (74.8%), followed by CTE Participants (65.0%) and CTE Concentrators or Completors (48.9%). This is the strongest and most clear association observed for CTE achievement across any outcome in this analysis, and it runs directly counter to the pattern observed for workforce participation — higher CTE engagement is strongly associated with sub-baccalaureate rather than bachelor degree or higher attainment among completers. This confirms that CTE pathways are primarily associated with shorter-term credential attainment rather than 4-year degree completion.
Continuous Variables - Ranked by Eta-Squared
1. ACT Composite Score (η²=0.167) The strongest continuous predictor with a large effect size — the largest observed for any continuous variable across all outcomes examined in this analysis. Bachelor degree or higher completers score substantially higher than sub-baccalaureate completers (estimate=3.887, p<0.001), confirming that ACT composite score is a powerful predictor of credential level among completers.
2. MCA Reading (η²=0.118) A medium to large effect size. Bachelor degree or higher completers score significantly higher than sub- baccalaureate completers (estimate=0.541, p<0.001), the largest MCA subject gap observed for this outcome.
3. MCA Science (η²=0.101) A medium effect size, noting the voluntary and self- selected nature of Science MCA participation. Bachelor degree or higher completers score significantly higher than sub-baccalaureate completers (estimate=0.526, p<0.001).
4. Total CTE Courses Taken (η²=0.084) A small to medium effect size — notably stronger than for previous outcomes — with sub-baccalaureate completers taking significantly more CTE courses than bachelor degree or higher completers (estimate=2.226, p<0.001). The direction of this effect is consistent with cte.achievement, confirming that higher CTE engagement is associated with sub-baccalaureate rather than bachelor degree or higher attainment among completers.
5. MCA Math (η²=0.081) A small to medium effect size closely mirroring MCA Reading and Science. Bachelor degree or higher completers score significantly higher than sub- baccalaureate completers (estimate=0.546, p<0.001).
Summary High school accomplishment variables show the strongest associations with credential level attained among college completers of any variable group examined for this outcome. ACT composite score emerges as the strongest predictor overall (η²=0.167 — a large effect), while took.ACT shows the strongest categorical association (φ=0.360). A critically important and substantively compelling finding is the clear and consistent inverse relationship between CTE engagement and bachelor degree or higher attainment — both cte.achievement and total CTE courses taken show meaningful associations with sub-baccalaureate rather than bachelor degree or higher credentials among completers. This is the strongest evidence yet that CTE and academic pathways represent distinct postsecondary trajectories, with CTE engagement strongly predicting shorter-term credential attainment even among those who do complete postsecondary education.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
Summary
Cross-tabulation analysis and one-way ANOVA examined associations between independent variables and postsecondary graduation institution sector (Public 4-year, Public 2-year, Private not-for-profit 4-year, Other college type) among the 24,998 college completers in the dataset. Variables are presented in two separate ranked lists by effect size measure. All categorical variables report Cramer’s V.
Categorical Variables - Ranked by Cramer’s V

took.ACT (Cramer’s V=0.381) — The strongest categorical predictor. Non-ACT completers are overwhelmingly concentrated in public 2-year institutions (75.2%), while ACT takers show much higher rates of public 4-year (46.1%) and private not-for-profit 4-year graduation (15.2%).
pseo.participant (Cramer’s V=0.322) — The second strongest categorical predictor. PSEO participants show notably higher rates of public 4-year (49.2%) and private not-for-profit 4-year graduation (15.7%), while non-participants are heavily concentrated in public 2-year institutions (55.4%).
ap.exam (Cramer’s V=0.290) — A moderate to strong association. AP exam participants show high rates of public 4-year (53.0%) and private not-for-profit 4-year graduation (24.6% — the highest of any categorical subgroup), while non-AP exam completers are concentrated in public 2-year institutions (42.8%).
special.ed.status (Cramer’s V=0.221) — The strongest demographic predictor. Special education completers are overwhelmingly concentrated in public 2-year institutions (78.6%) with virtually no representation in private not-for-profit 4-year institutions (2.4%).
economic.status (Cramer’s V=0.195) — The second strongest demographic predictor. Economically disadvantaged completers show much higher public 2-year rates (51.7% vs 30.9%) and lower public 4-year rates (29.0% vs 44.0%).
cte.achievement (Cramer’s V=0.167) — A moderate association with a clear dose-response pattern. CTE Concentrators or Completors show the highest public 2-year rate (46.8%) while No CTE completers show the highest private not-for-profit 4-year (20.3%) and public 4-year rates (47.0%).
english.learner (Cramer’s V=0.155) — A weak to moderate association. English learner completers show a strikingly high public 2-year rate (69.8%) and very low private not-for-profit 4-year rate (3.9%).
gender (Cramer’s V=0.151) — A weak to moderate association. Males show considerably higher public 2-year rates (42.7% vs 30.4%) while females show higher rates across all 4-year institution types.
non.english.home (Cramer’s V=0.124) — A weak association mirroring english.learner. Students from non-English speaking homes show high public 2-year rates (60.3%) and low private not-for-profit 4-year rates (6.3%).
race.ethnicity (Cramer’s V=0.069) — A very weak association. Hispanic completers show the highest public 2-year rate (57.6%) while White completers show the highest public 4-year rate (43.0%).
edr (Cramer’s V=0.079) — A very weak association. EDR 6E Southwest Central completers show the highest private not-for-profit 4-year rate (17.1%) while EDR 6W Upper Minnesota Valley shows the highest public 2-year rate (43.1%).
dem.desc (Cramer’s V=0.057) — A very weak association. Urban/town/rural mix completers show the highest public 4-year rate (45.0%) while entirely rural completers show the highest public 2-year rate (39.8%).

Continuous Variables - Ranked by Eta-Squared

ACT Composite Score (η²=0.199) — A large effect size — the largest observed for any continuous variable across the entire postsecondary pathway analysis. Private not-for-profit 4-year graduates score substantially higher than all other groups, with a gap of 5.411 points between private not-for-profit 4-year and public 2-year graduates — the largest single group difference observed for any continuous variable in this analysis.
MCA Reading (η²=0.130) — A medium to large effect. Private not-for-profit 4-year graduates score highest while public 2-year graduates score the lowest, with a gap of 0.650 between these groups.
MCA Science (η²=0.122) — A medium effect, noting the voluntary nature of participation. The ordering across institution types mirrors Reading and ACT composite throughout.
Total CTE Courses Taken (η²=0.096) — A small to medium effect with the most distinctive pattern — public 2-year graduates show significantly more CTE courses than all other groups (estimate=3.065 vs private not-for-profit 4-year), confirming the CTE-to-community-college pathway at the institutional level.
MCA Math (η²=0.092) — A small to medium effect mirroring Reading and Science. Private not-for-profit 4-year graduates score highest and public 2-year graduates score the lowest.
avg.unemployment.rate (η²=0.008) — A negligible effect. Public 2-year graduates experienced significantly lower unemployment rates than other institution type graduates.
avg.wages.pct.state (η²=0.002) — A negligible effect. Local wage levels explain virtually no variance in institution type among completers.

Overall Pattern The predictors of institution sector among college completers show the strongest associations observed across the entire postsecondary pathway analysis, with ACT composite score producing the largest effect size of any continuous variable examined (η²=0.199). The institutional sorting by academic achievement and CTE engagement is remarkably clear and consistent across every variable group examined — high academic achievers graduate from private not-for-profit and public 4-year institutions, while lower academic achievers and higher CTE engagers who do complete postsecondary do so almost exclusively at public 2-year institutions. Demographic disadvantage variables show strong concentrations in public 2-year institutions across special education status, economic status, English learner status, and non-English home language. Geographic variables remain very weak, confirming that individual-level characteristics overwhelmingly determine institution type among college completers in Southwest Minnesota. The two-pathway structure — academic to 4-year and CTE to community college — that has been a consistent theme throughout this analysis is confirmed most definitively by this institution sector outcome.
